vpc.title: VPC
vpc.body: A Virtual Private Cloud is your own fenced-off region of the AWS network. Nothing gets in or out unless you build a way. Inside it, subnets divide the space; each subnet sits in one Availability Zone.
simplifications: The game has one VPC with fixed subnets. Real VPCs can be laid out any way you like.

internet-gateway.title: Internet Gateway
internet-gateway.body: The gate between your VPC and the internet. Attaching one is not enough on its own: a subnet only becomes public when its route table sends internet traffic (0.0.0.0/0) to the gateway.

route-table.title: Route table
route-table.body: A list of signposts for traffic leaving a subnet. Every route table has a local route for the VPC that cannot be removed. When several routes match, the most specific one wins.
simplifications: Destinations are named choices (Internet, S3, DynamoDB) rather than address ranges you type.

load-balancer.title: Application Load Balancer
load-balancer.body: The front door. It receives web requests and shares them between healthy targets, across Availability Zones. An internet-facing load balancer lives in public subnets in at least two zones.
simplifications: Targets always receive traffic on HTTP 80; the load balancer handles HTTPS (certificates are assumed).
One listener and one set of targets. Real load balancers can have several, with rules.
Health is judged instantly. Real health checks take a few intervals to change their mind.
The load balancer itself never runs out of capacity. Real ones scale automatically, but a sudden spike can briefly outpace them.

security-group.title: Security group
security-group.body: A firewall worn by a resource: the pencilled outline around a cloud. It holds allow rules only; anything not allowed is refused. It is stateful: the reply to an allowed request is always let through. A rule's source can be another security group, meaning "anything wearing that group".
simplifications: Ports are picked from a short list of named choices.

network-acl.title: Network ACL
network-acl.body: A fence on a subnet's boundary. Rules are numbered and read lowest first; the first match decides, and it can allow or deny. It is stateless: replies need their own rule, usually for ephemeral ports 1024–65535.
simplifications: Sources are "anywhere" or one of a few named address ranges.
Replies are checked against one representative ephemeral port.

ec2-instance.title: EC2 instance
ec2-instance.body: A virtual server. It lives in exactly one subnet, wears security groups, and can be given an IAM role so the software on it can call other AWS services without any stored keys.
simplifications: Instances in the game never have public addresses, so nothing on the ground can reach them directly.
Machine images and instance families are left out.

nat-gateway.title: NAT Gateway
nat-gateway.body: A one-way door. It sits in a public subnet and lets resources in private subnets start connections out to the internet. It never lets the internet start a connection in. It lives in one Availability Zone, and it is charged by the hour and by the gigabyte.

s3-bucket.title: S3 bucket
s3-bucket.body: Object storage, outside your VPC, holding as much as you care to put in it. Block Public Access is on by default and overrides any policy that would open the bucket to everyone. Every new object is encrypted at rest by default.
simplifications: Block Public Access is one switch here; in AWS it is four related settings.
Bucket policies can grant to everyone or to a named role, nothing finer.

iam-role.title: IAM role
iam-role.body: A set of permissions that a resource can wear. IAM denies everything by default; a statement must explicitly allow an action, and an explicit deny beats any allow. Grant only what is used: that is least privilege.
simplifications: Permissions are grouped into families such as s3:Read and s3:Write, on one resource or on everything (*).
There are no users or access keys in the game: only roles.

concept-public-subnet.title: What makes a subnet public?
concept-public-subnet.body: One thing only: its route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 to an Internet Gateway attached to the VPC. Not its name, not its position. And even then, a security group must allow each connection in.

concept-security-group-chaining.title: Chaining security groups
concept-security-group-chaining.body: Instead of allowing an address range, a rule can name another security group. "Allow HTTP from the load balancer's group" stays correct however many load balancer nodes there are and whatever their addresses. Each tier trusts only the tier in front of it.

concept-roles-not-keys.title: Roles, not keys
concept-roles-not-keys.body: Software on an instance gets its permissions from the instance's IAM role: short-lived credentials that AWS hands out and rotates. Nothing secret is stored on the server. Without a role, the instance cannot sign a request at all.

gateway-endpoint.title: Gateway endpoint
gateway-endpoint.body: A private road from your VPC to S3 or DynamoDB. It is not a thing you place in a subnet: it appears as a route in the route table, with a prefix list (the service's address ranges) as the destination. Because that route is more specific than 0.0.0.0/0, traffic for the service takes it and never leaves the AWS network. Gateway endpoints exist for S3 and DynamoDB only, and have no additional charge.
simplifications: Endpoint policies, which can restrict what the endpoint may be used for, are left out.
In AWS you create the endpoint and choose route tables for it; here you add the route directly.

concept-cost.title: Paying for what you leave running
concept-cost.body: Some resources cost money for every hour they exist, whether or not anything uses them. A NAT Gateway is one: it is charged by the hour and by the gigabyte. A gateway endpoint to S3 costs nothing. Choosing the cheaper path that still does the job is part of building well.
simplifications: Coins are illustrative units for comparing choices. They are not real AWS prices.

auto-scaling-group.title: Auto Scaling group
auto-scaling-group.body: A fleet of identical EC2 instances with a minimum, a maximum and a desired size. It spreads its instances across the subnets you choose, and so across Availability Zones. With a scaling policy it changes its own size: a target tracking policy keeps a measure such as average CPU near a target, launching instances when the fleet is busy and removing them when it is quiet. Attached to a load balancer, its instances register as targets automatically.
simplifications: Each Cloudling keeps one kite up, and every instance has room for a fixed number of kites by size (5, 10 or 20). A new instance takes 2 minutes to start serving. Real launch times and capacities vary.
Only target tracking on CPU is offered. Step, simple, scheduled and predictive scaling are left out.

When CPU has stayed below the target for 2 minutes, the group removes enough instances to bring it back up to the target, but never more than half the fleet at once. AWS also scales in more gradually than out, at a pace it decides itself.
A kite that finds every target busy times out in the same tick. Real requests wait in a queue first, and some are served late.
Every kite in a crowd is treated alike, so one journey stands for all of them.
A group keeps at least one instance; AWS allows a minimum of zero.
Launch templates, health-check replacement and instance warm-up settings are left out.
A group can have at most 16 instances here, so the sky can draw every one. Real groups can be far larger.

cloudwatch.title: CloudWatch
cloudwatch.body: The weather station. CloudWatch collects metrics, such as the CPU use of a fleet or the number of requests at a load balancer, and alarms watch a metric against a threshold. An alarm is either OK or in ALARM, and can trigger an action such as scaling a group. With a target tracking policy, EC2 Auto Scaling creates and manages the alarms for you.
simplifications: Metrics are measured once a minute, and an alarm acts on a single reading: above the target at once, below it after 2 minutes. Real alarms wait for several readings, and the scale-in alarm waits much longer.
CPU is modelled as the share of the targets' room in use: kites ÷ room.

concept-elasticity.title: Elasticity
concept-elasticity.body: Matching capacity to demand as demand changes: more when it is busy, less when it is quiet, without anyone doing it by hand. It is one of the main reasons to build in the cloud. The alternative is to buy for the busiest day and pay for that capacity on every other day.

concept-cidr.title: What does /16 mean?
concept-cidr.body: An address range is written as a starting address and a number after the slash, called CIDR notation. An IPv4 address has 32 bits; the number says how many of them are fixed. The rest are free to vary, so a smaller number means a bigger range, and each step down doubles it.
points: /16: 65,536 addresses. 10.0.0.0/16 runs from 10.0.0.0 to 10.0.255.255. This is the largest range AWS allows for a VPC, and the size of this one.
/24: 256 addresses, e.g. 10.0.1.0 to 10.0.1.255. Each subnet here is a /24 carved out of the VPC's range. AWS keeps the first four and the last address of every subnet, so 251 are yours.
/28: 16 addresses. The smallest range AWS allows for a VPC or a subnet.
/32: exactly one address. Too small for a subnet; used in rules to name a single machine, e.g. 203.0.113.10/32.
/0: every address. 0.0.0.0/0 is the "Internet" or "Anywhere" in routes and rules.
A subnet's range must sit inside its VPC's range, and subnets in one VPC must not overlap.
simplifications: The game never asks you to work out ranges: the VPC and subnets come ready-made, and IPv6 is left out.

concept-listener.title: Listener
concept-listener.body: A listener is the load balancer's ear. It waits for connections on one protocol and port, such as HTTPS 443, and passes the requests it hears on to the targets. The security group must allow the same port, or a request never reaches the listener.
points: HTTPS 443 encrypts the conversation between the Cloudling and the load balancer. HTTP 80 sends it in the clear, where anyone on the way could read it.

In real life, an HTTPS listener needs an SSL/TLS certificate deployed on the load balancer. The certificate proves the website is really yours. AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) can issue one and renew it for you.
The load balancer decrypts each request and sends it on to its targets. Here the targets always receive HTTP 80, inside the VPC.
simplifications: Certificates are assumed: the game never asks you to request or attach one.
One listener per load balancer, with no listener rules.

concept-bastion-host.title: Bastion host
concept-bastion-host.body: A bastion host, or jump box, is the traditional way for people to reach EC2 instances that have no public address. It is a small EC2 instance in a public subnet. An administrator connects to it first, usually with SSH on port 22, and from there connects on to the EC2 instance in the private subnet.
points: The bastion's security group allows SSH only from known addresses, such as an office's range, never from Anywhere.
The private EC2 instances allow SSH only from the bastion's security group: the same chaining as the load balancer and the application servers.
Each hop needs credentials, usually an SSH key pair. An attacker would need the bastion's address and those keys; the red Cloudling has neither.
A bastion is a target in its own right, so it has to be patched, watched and kept small.
AWS also offers a way to do without one: Systems Manager Session Manager needs no open inbound ports, no bastion host and no SSH keys. Access is controlled with IAM, and sessions can be logged.
simplifications: There is no bastion host in these levels: nothing here needs anyone to log in to an EC2 instance.
